ix: Introduction to Capital Market
Which feature best distinguishes the primary market from the secondary market?
Securities are issued for the first time and the issuer receives the money
Only listed securities are traded between existing investors
Prices are always fixed by SEBI rather than by demand and supply
Only institutional investors are permitted to participate
In the primary market, new securities are created and sold so funds flow to the issuer; secondary market trades happen between investors.
Introduction to Capital Market
Under which statute did SEBI acquire statutory powers to regulate the Indian securities market?
The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956
The Depositories Act, 1996
The Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992
The Companies Act, 2013
SEBI was set up in 1988 as a non-statutory body and received statutory powers through the SEBI Act, 1992.
Introduction to Capital Market
A company already listed on a stock exchange offers fresh shares to the public. What is this issue called?
Initial public offer (IPO)
Further public offer (FPO)
Private placement
Bonus issue
A public issue of fresh securities by an issuer that is already listed is a further public offer; an IPO is by an unlisted issuer.
Introduction to Capital Market
Which of the following is a function of a depository in the Indian capital market?
Guaranteeing the settlement of trades executed on the exchange
Fixing the issue price of securities in a public issue
Providing credit ratings for debt instruments
Holding securities in dematerialised form and effecting transfers by book entry
Depositories (NSDL and CDSL) hold securities electronically and transfer them by book entry; settlement guarantee is the clearing corporation's role.
Introduction to Merchant Banking
Under the SEBI (Merchant Bankers) Regulations, 1992, the core activity that defines a merchant banker is:
Accepting public deposits and granting loans to corporates
Holding securities in electronic form on behalf of investors
Issue management, including arranging the selling, buying or subscription of securities and acting as manager, consultant or adviser
Executing trades on a stock exchange on behalf of clients
The regulations define a merchant banker by its issue-management business; deposit taking, custody and broking are other activities.
Introduction to Merchant Banking
Which of these services is typically offered by a merchant banker?
Advising a company on the structure and timing of a capital-raising issue
Issuing currency notes on behalf of the government
Acting as the depository for a listed company's shares
Running the clearing and settlement system of a stock exchange
Merchant bankers advise on and manage capital-raising; currency issue, depository and clearing functions belong to other institutions.
Introduction to Merchant Banking
A merchant banker that acts as the lead manager to a public issue is commonly called the:
Registrar to the issue
Sponsor bank
Debenture trustee
Book running lead manager (BRLM)
The lead manager that manages the book-building process is the BRLM; the registrar, sponsor bank and trustee perform separate roles.
Introduction to Merchant Banking
Why does SEBI require a merchant banker to be involved in a public issue of securities?
To guarantee investors a minimum return on the issue
To ensure professional due diligence and disclosure so that investors receive accurate information
To replace the board of directors of the issuer during the issue
To fix the market price of the shares after listing
The merchant banker's due diligence and disclosure role protects investors; it does not guarantee returns or control post-listing prices.
Registration, Code of Conduct & Obligations
Which of the following is permitted to act as a merchant banker in India?
Any chartered accountant in practice without SEBI registration
A body corporate registered with SEBI as a merchant banker
Any listed company for its own issues without registration
An individual investor with a demat account
No one can carry on merchant banking activity without a certificate of registration from SEBI, and registration is granted to body corporates.
Registration, Code of Conduct & Obligations
A merchant banker discovers that it is an associate of the issuer whose IPO it has been asked to lead manage. What should it do?
Act as lead manager after disclosing the relationship in the red herring prospectus
Act as lead manager if the issue size is small
Act as lead manager after taking approval from the stock exchange
Decline to act as lead manager, because a merchant banker cannot lead manage an issue of an associate
The regulations bar a merchant banker from lead managing an issue where it is an associate of the issuer, to avoid conflicts of interest; disclosure does not cure this.
Registration, Code of Conduct & Obligations
The SEBI-mandated code of conduct requires a merchant banker to:
Act with integrity, due skill, care and diligence and avoid conflicts of interest
Promise investors a guaranteed listing gain
Share confidential client information with other clients to improve pricing
Recommend only issues on which it earns the highest fee
The code of conduct centres on integrity, diligence, fairness to clients and managing conflicts; promising returns or misusing information is prohibited.
Registration, Code of Conduct & Obligations
Which officer must a SEBI-registered merchant banker appoint to monitor compliance with securities laws and to redress investor grievances?
Statutory auditor
Registrar to the issue
Compliance officer
Debenture trustee
A merchant banker must appoint a compliance officer responsible for monitoring compliance with SEBI rules and handling investor grievances.
Registration, Code of Conduct & Obligations
An employee of a merchant banker learns of a pending, unannounced acquisition by a client company and buys its shares. This is:
Insider trading, prohibited under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015
Permitted, as long as the employee holds the shares for at least one year
Permitted, because the merchant banker itself did not trade
A matter only for the company's internal disciplinary policy
Trading while in possession of unpublished price sensitive information is insider trading, regardless of holding period or who placed the trade.
Registration, Code of Conduct & Obligations
SEBI finds that a merchant banker has failed to carry out due diligence in an issue. Which action is SEBI empowered to take?
Only issue an advisory letter, as SEBI cannot penalise intermediaries
Refer the matter to the stock exchange, which alone can act
Initiate enforcement action such as a penalty, suspension or cancellation of registration
Order the issuer to replace its statutory auditor
SEBI can impose monetary penalties and suspend or cancel registration of an intermediary that violates its regulations.
Issue Management – Important Terms
What does the term 'red herring prospectus' (RHP) refer to in a book-built issue?
A prospectus filed after the issue has closed containing allotment details
An offer document that does not contain the final price or the exact number of shares offered
A document used only for private placements to QIBs
A prospectus that SEBI has rejected
The RHP carries all disclosures except the final price and quantity, which are determined through book building and appear in the final prospectus.
Issue Management – Important Terms
In a book-built public issue, who is permitted to bid at the 'cut-off' price?
Qualified institutional buyers
Non-institutional investors applying above ₹2 lakh
Anchor investors
Retail individual investors (and eligible employee/shareholder reservation categories)
The cut-off option is available only to retail individual investors and certain reserved categories; QIBs and NIIs must bid at a specific price.
Issue Management – Important Terms
As per SEBI ICDR, a 'retail individual investor' is an individual who applies for securities of value:
Not more than ₹5 lakh
Not more than ₹10 lakh
Not more than ₹2 lakh
Not more than ₹1 lakh
ICDR defines a retail individual investor as one applying for not more than ₹2 lakh in an issue; applications above that fall in the non-institutional category.
Issue Management – Important Terms
In a book-built issue, the cap of the price band must not exceed what percentage of the floor price?
Under ICDR, the cap of the price band cannot be more than 120% of the floor price.
Issue Management – Important Terms
An IPO consists entirely of shares sold by existing shareholders. What is this component called and who receives the proceeds?
Fresh issue; the company receives the proceeds
Rights issue; the company receives the proceeds
Bonus issue; no money is received by anyone
Offer for sale; the selling shareholders receive the proceeds
In an offer for sale, existing shareholders sell their shares, so proceeds go to them and not to the company.
Issue Management – Important Terms
Which statement about a 'shelf prospectus' is correct?
It is a prospectus kept confidential and never filed with SEBI
It allows an eligible issuer to make one or more issues over a validity period without filing a fresh prospectus each time
It is required only for bonus issues
It replaces the need for any disclosure of material changes
A shelf prospectus enables multiple issues during its validity period; issuers file an information memorandum or addendum for material changes.
Issue Management – Important Terms
'Anchor investors' in a main-board book-built IPO are drawn from which category?
Retail individual investors
Qualified institutional buyers
Employees of the issuer
Promoters of the issuer
Anchor investors are QIBs to whom a part of the QIB portion is allocated before the issue opens.
Issue Management – Important Terms
What is a 'green shoe option' in a public issue?
An option for promoters to buy back shares at the issue price after listing
A discount offered to retail investors on the issue price
An option to extend the issue period indefinitely
An over-allotment option used by a stabilising agent to support the post-listing price
The green shoe option permits over-allotment, with a stabilising agent using the proceeds to buy shares in the market if the price falls below the issue price.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
Which of the following is one of the eligibility tests under Regulation 6(1) of SEBI ICDR for a main-board IPO?
An average operating profit of at least ₹15 crore during the preceding three years, with operating profit in each of those years
A net worth of at least ₹100 crore in each of the preceding five years
A minimum of 10,000 shareholders before filing the draft offer document
A track record of dividends for ten consecutive years
Regulation 6(1) requires net tangible assets, an operating profit track record (average ₹15 crore over three years with profit each year) and net worth tests.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
An unlisted company does not meet the profitability track record test of Regulation 6(1). Under Regulation 6(2) it can still do an IPO if:
Its promoters contribute 50% of the post-issue capital
It lists only on a regional stock exchange
At least 75% of the net offer is allotted to qualified institutional buyers
It obtains a guarantee from a scheduled commercial bank
Regulation 6(2) allows issuers not meeting 6(1) to make an IPO through book building if at least 75% of the net offer goes to QIBs.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
Under ICDR, the minimum promoter contribution in an IPO is:
20% of the post-issue capital
10% of the pre-issue capital
51% of the post-issue capital
25% of the issue size
Promoters must hold at least 20% of the post-issue capital as minimum promoter contribution, which is subject to lock-in.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
In a main-board IPO whose objects do not involve capital expenditure, the minimum promoter contribution is locked in for:
6 months from the date of allotment
3 years from the date of allotment
18 months from the date of allotment
5 years from the date of allotment
Since 2021 the lock-in on minimum promoter contribution is 18 months (3 years where objects involve capital expenditure for a project).
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
A public issue has failed to receive minimum subscription of 90% of the fresh issue. What must happen?
The lead manager must allot shares to itself at a discount
The application money must be refunded to applicants
The issue period is extended automatically by 30 days
Shares are allotted proportionately to whoever applied
If minimum subscription of 90% of the fresh issue is not received, the issuer must refund the entire application money within the prescribed time.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
In the standard book-building allocation for an issuer eligible under Regulation 6(1), the QIB portion can be:
Not less than 75% of the net offer
Exactly 35% of the net offer
Not more than 10% of the net offer
Not more than 50% of the net offer
For a 6(1) issuer, ICDR caps QIB allocation at 50% of the net offer, with minimum allocations to non-institutional and retail investors.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
How long must a public issue remain open for bidding under ICDR, in the normal course?
Exactly one working day
At least ten working days and not more than thirty days
At least three working days and not more than ten working days
Until the issue is fully subscribed, without any limit
ICDR requires an issue to be kept open for a minimum of three working days and a maximum of ten working days.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
What is the current timeline, after issue closure, by which shares in a public issue must be listed?
T+3 working days, where T is the issue closing date
T+6 working days
T+12 working days
T+30 calendar days
SEBI made the T+3 listing timeline mandatory for public issues from December 2023, reducing it from T+6.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
In an underwriting arrangement for a public issue, 'devolvement' means:
The issuer cancels the issue for lack of demand
The stock exchange lists the securities before allotment
Shares are transferred from promoters to the public
The underwriter must subscribe to the unsubscribed portion it has underwritten
When the issue is undersubscribed, the shortfall devolves on the underwriter, who must take up the unsubscribed securities as per its commitment.
Issue Management – Process & Underwriting
Which applicants in a public issue must apply only through ASBA (Application Supported by Blocked Amount)?
Only retail individual investors
All applicants other than anchor investors
Only qualified institutional buyers
Only non-resident investors
ASBA is mandatory for all investors in public issues, with anchor investors being the exception as they apply directly to the BRLMs.
Issue Management – Obligations & Due Diligence
The due diligence certificate in a public issue is submitted to SEBI by:
The registrar to the issue
The lead manager(s) to the issue
The bankers to the issue
The stock exchange
The lead manager files a due diligence certificate confirming that disclosures in the offer document are true, fair and adequate.
Issue Management – Obligations & Due Diligence
The draft offer document filed with SEBI is made public for comments for at least:
7 days
45 days
90 days
21 days
ICDR requires the draft offer document to be kept open for public comments for a period of at least 21 days from filing.
Issue Management – Obligations & Due Diligence
After SEBI issues its observations on a draft offer document, within what period must the issue open?
12 months from the date of SEBI's observations
3 months from the date of SEBI's observations
24 months from the date of filing the draft
There is no time limit
An issuer must open the issue within 12 months of SEBI's observations, failing which it must file a fresh draft offer document.
Issue Management – Obligations & Due Diligence
In an IPO, the amount raised for 'general corporate purposes' cannot exceed:
50% of the gross proceeds of the issue
10% of the net worth of the issuer
25% of the gross proceeds of the issue
75% of the fresh issue
ICDR caps the amount that can be earmarked for general corporate purposes at 25% of the gross proceeds.
Issue Management – Obligations & Due Diligence
What is the role of a monitoring agency appointed in a public issue?
To monitor the use of issue proceeds against the objects stated in the offer document
To stabilise the share price after listing
To underwrite the unsubscribed portion
To verify the KYC of each applicant
The monitoring agency reports on how the issue proceeds are actually used compared with the stated objects.
Issue Management – Obligations & Due Diligence
While performing due diligence, the lead manager finds an undisclosed pending litigation that could materially affect the issuer. The best course is:
Ignore it if the issuer's management says it will be settled
Mention it only in an internal file note
Ensure the litigation and its possible impact are disclosed in the offer document before proceeding
Withdraw from the issue without informing anyone
The lead manager must ensure all material information is disclosed so that investors can take an informed decision.
Issue Management – Obligations & Due Diligence
Which statement about the merchant banker's role after the issue closes is correct?
Its responsibilities end the moment bidding closes
It continues to coordinate post-issue activities such as basis of allotment, refunds and listing
It becomes responsible for paying dividends to investors
It takes over as the company secretary of the issuer
The lead manager remains responsible for post-issue activities including finalisation of allotment, refunds, credit of shares and listing.
Mergers, Acquisitions & Takeovers
Under the SEBI (SAST) Regulations, 2011, an acquirer must make an open offer when it acquires shares or voting rights entitling it to:
10% or more of the voting rights
51% or more of the voting rights
5% or more of the voting rights
25% or more of the voting rights in the target company
Regulation 3(1) of SAST triggers a mandatory open offer when an acquirer crosses 25% of voting rights.
Mergers, Acquisitions & Takeovers
An acquirer already holds 30% of a listed company. Without making an open offer, how much more can it acquire in a financial year under the creeping acquisition route?
Up to 10% of the voting rights
Up to 15% of the voting rights
Up to 5% of the voting rights
Up to 25% of the voting rights
An acquirer holding between 25% and the maximum permissible non-public shareholding can acquire up to 5% per financial year without an open offer.
Mergers, Acquisitions & Takeovers
The minimum size of a mandatory open offer under SAST is:
26% of the total shares of the target company
20% of the total shares
51% of the total shares
15% of the total shares
A mandatory open offer must be for at least 26% of the total shares of the target company.
Mergers, Acquisitions & Takeovers
Who must the acquirer appoint to manage an open offer under SAST?
The statutory auditor of the target company
Any stock broker registered with the exchange
The company secretary of the target company
A SEBI-registered merchant banker who is not an associate of the acquirer
The manager to the open offer must be a SEBI-registered merchant banker independent of the acquirer.
Mergers, Acquisitions & Takeovers
In an open offer, the acquirer must open an escrow account. For an offer consideration of ₹600 crore, what is the minimum escrow?
₹150 crore
₹135 crore
₹60 crore
₹125 crore
Escrow is 25% of the first ₹500 crore (₹125 crore) plus 10% of the balance ₹100 crore (₹10 crore), totalling ₹135 crore.
Mergers, Acquisitions & Takeovers
Under SAST, a person holding 5% or more of a listed company's shares must make a disclosure when the holding changes by:
0.5% or more
2% or more of the total shareholding or voting rights
10% or more
Any change, however small, every day
Regulation 29 requires disclosure on reaching 5% and thereafter on every change of 2% or more.
Disinvestment & Buyback
Under the Companies Act, 2013, a buyback approved only by the board of directors (without a special resolution) is limited to:
25% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves
5% of the paid-up equity capital only
50% of the free reserves
10% of the total paid-up equity capital and free reserves
Section 68 allows a board-approved buyback up to 10% of paid-up equity capital and free reserves; above that, a special resolution is needed (overall cap 25%).
Disinvestment & Buyback
Post-buyback, the ratio of a company's aggregate secured and unsecured debt to its paid-up capital and free reserves generally cannot exceed:
Section 68 of the Companies Act requires the post-buyback debt-equity ratio to be not more than 2:1 (unless a higher ratio is notified for a class of companies).
Disinvestment & Buyback
A company completed a buyback eight months ago. Can it make a fresh buyback offer now?
Yes, there is no gap required between buybacks
Yes, provided the new buyback is under 5% of capital
No, a fresh buyback cannot be made within one year of the closure of the previous buyback offer
Yes, if the stock exchange approves
The Companies Act prohibits a buyback offer within one year from the closure of the preceding buyback offer.
Disinvestment & Buyback
Which method of buyback involves the company offering to buy shares from all shareholders on a proportionate basis at a fixed price?
Tender offer
Open market purchase through stock exchange
Private placement
Odd-lot purchase
In a tender offer, the company offers to buy shares from existing shareholders proportionately at a specified price.
Disinvestment & Buyback
In India, which department of the Government of India handles disinvestment of the Centre's stake in public sector enterprises?
Department of Economic Affairs, Capital Markets Division
Reserve Bank of India
Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM)
Department of Financial Services
DIPAM, under the Ministry of Finance, manages the Government's disinvestment programme and equity in CPSEs.
xxiii: Social Sector Ecosystem
How many Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) were adopted by the United Nations under the 2030 Agenda?
The 2030 Agenda adopted in 2015 contains 17 SDGs, succeeding the 8 Millennium Development Goals.
Social Sector Ecosystem
Which of the following is a typical legal form of a not-for-profit organisation in India?
A limited liability partnership distributing profits to partners
A private limited company paying dividends
A company registered under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013
A sole proprietorship
Trusts, societies and Section 8 companies are the main NPO forms; they cannot distribute profits to members.
Social Sector Ecosystem
Under Section 135 of the Companies Act, 2013, a company meeting the CSR thresholds must spend on CSR in a financial year at least:
5% of its turnover of the preceding year
2% of its average net profits of the three immediately preceding financial years
1% of its net worth
10% of its dividend payout
Section 135 requires qualifying companies to spend at least 2% of average net profits of the preceding three years on CSR activities.
Social Sector Ecosystem
'Impact investing' is best described as:
Donating money with no expectation of any outcome
Investing only in government bonds
Short-term trading in shares of large companies
Investing with the intention to generate measurable social or environmental impact alongside a financial return
Impact investors seek intentional, measurable positive impact together with financial return, distinguishing them from pure philanthropy.
SSE: Introduction, Funding Structures & Instruments
The Social Stock Exchange (SSE) in India operates as:
A new stock exchange owned by the Government
A department of the Reserve Bank of India
A separate segment of a recognised stock exchange
A wing of NITI Aayog that grants funds
SEBI's framework sets up the SSE as a separate segment of an existing recognised stock exchange, such as those of BSE and NSE.
SSE: Introduction, Funding Structures & Instruments
Which two types of 'Social Enterprises' can access the Social Stock Exchange?
Not-for-profit organisations (NPOs) and for-profit social enterprises (FPEs)
Listed banks and insurance companies
Political parties and religious organisations
Mutual funds and portfolio managers
The SSE framework recognises NPOs and FPEs with social intent and impact as Social Enterprises.
SSE: Introduction, Funding Structures & Instruments
A Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP) instrument issued by an NPO on the SSE:
Pays a fixed coupon but no principal
Repays principal at maturity with no coupon
Converts into equity shares of the NPO
Pays no interest and does not repay the principal at maturity
ZCZP instruments are effectively donations through the exchange: investors receive neither coupon nor principal, but receive impact reporting.
SSE: Introduction, Funding Structures & Instruments
Which instrument can a for-profit social enterprise use to raise funds through the SSE route?
Zero Coupon Zero Principal instruments
Equity shares through the main board, SME platform or Innovators Growth Platform
Donations through mutual fund schemes only
Government grants routed via the exchange
FPEs raise funds like other companies, for example through equity or debt issues; ZCZP instruments are available only to NPOs.
SSE: Introduction, Funding Structures & Instruments
Which of the following entities is NOT eligible to be identified as a Social Enterprise under the SSE framework?
A Section 8 company working on child education for low-income families
A corporate foundation
A registered trust providing healthcare to tribal communities
A for-profit firm providing livelihood support to small farmers as its main activity
The ICDR excludes corporate foundations, political or religious organisations, professional or trade associations and most infrastructure/housing companies.
SSE: Introduction, Funding Structures & Instruments
Under the SSE framework, an entity must show social intent by targeting underserved or less privileged populations. At least what share of its activities should be eligible social activities?
25%, measured by number of employees
51%, measured by share capital
100% of all activities without exception
67%, measured by revenue, expenditure or beneficiaries (3-year average)
An entity must demonstrate that at least 67% of its activities (by revenue, expenditure or customer/beneficiary base over the preceding three years) are eligible activities.
Registration and Listing on SSE
Why does an NPO need to register on the Social Stock Exchange before raising funds through it?
Registration is a prerequisite for an NPO to issue securities such as ZCZP instruments on the SSE
Registration automatically lists its shares on the main board
Registration exempts it from all income-tax obligations
Registration converts it into a for-profit company
An NPO must first register with the SSE segment; only then can it raise funds through instruments like ZCZP.
Registration and Listing on SSE
An NPO registered on the SSE has not raised any funds through the exchange. Which statement is correct?
It has no obligations at all until it raises funds
It must delist immediately
It still has ongoing disclosure obligations as a registered NPO
It must convert into a for-profit enterprise
Registration carries annual disclosure obligations even if the NPO has not yet raised funds through the SSE.
Registration and Listing on SSE
A for-profit social enterprise wishes to list its equity shares. Which statement is correct?
It must meet the listing requirements applicable to the platform it lists on, in addition to the SSE social impact requirements
It is exempt from all listing requirements because it is a social enterprise
It can list only ZCZP instruments
It can list only on a foreign exchange
FPEs follow the ICDR and listing requirements of the relevant board, together with the additional social-intent and impact-reporting norms.
Registration and Listing on SSE
Which document must an NPO issuing ZCZP instruments on the SSE file with the exchange?
A red herring prospectus with price band
A takeover open-offer letter
A fund-raising document with disclosures such as vision, objectives, programmes, risks and proposed use of funds
A buyback letter of offer
NPOs raising funds through ZCZP issue a fund-raising document containing prescribed disclosures, including details of the projects and planned use of funds.
Registration and Listing on SSE
An NPO wants to register on the SSE. Which of these would be a basic eligibility consideration?
A minimum paid-up equity capital of ₹10 crore
Valid registration as an NPO and registration under income-tax law that grants it exemption, with a track record of operations
Positive net profits in each of the last five years
A credit rating of AA or above
NPO registration on SSE looks at legal registration, income-tax registration and track record; profit or equity capital tests do not apply to NPOs.
Registration and Listing on SSE
What happens to the funds that investors contribute through a ZCZP issue on the SSE?
They are held by the exchange and returned with interest
They are invested in equity shares on behalf of the investors
They are transferred to SEBI's Investor Protection Fund
They are used by the NPO for the specified social project, and the NPO reports on utilisation and impact
ZCZP funds go to the NPO for the stated project, and the NPO must disclose fund utilisation and social impact.
Logic Model in Social Programs
In a logic model, which is the correct sequence?
Outputs → Inputs → Activities → Impact → Outcomes
Activities → Impact → Inputs → Outputs → Outcomes
Inputs → Activities → Outputs → Outcomes → Impact
Impact → Outcomes → Outputs → Activities → Inputs
A logic model links resources (inputs) to activities, their direct products (outputs), resulting changes (outcomes) and long-term change (impact).
Logic Model in Social Programs
An NGO runs a skilling programme. 'Number of youth who completed the 3-month training' is an example of:
An output
An input
An impact
An assumption
Outputs are the direct, countable products of activities; outcomes would be changes such as youth getting jobs.
Logic Model in Social Programs
In the same skilling programme, '60% of trained youth secured jobs within six months and increased household income' is best classified as:
An input
An activity
An output
An outcome
Outcomes are the changes experienced by beneficiaries as a result of outputs, such as employment and income gains.
Logic Model in Social Programs
How is a 'theory of change' related to a logic model?
It is a financial statement showing the NGO's income
It explains the causal pathway and assumptions behind why the activities are expected to lead to the desired change
It lists only the inputs used
It replaces the need to measure any outcomes
A theory of change articulates the causal logic and assumptions; the logic model is often a concise representation of that pathway.
Social Impact Assessment & Assessors
Under the SSE framework, who may carry out the social impact assessment of a Social Enterprise?
Any employee of the Social Enterprise
A social auditor registered with a self-regulatory organisation and holding the NISM social impact assessor certification
The stock exchange's listing department
A credit rating agency without any certification
Social impact assessment is done by social auditors who are members of an SRO under a recognised professional institute and hold the required NISM certification.
Social Impact Assessment & Assessors
A social auditor is asked to assess an NPO where her brother is the chief executive. What should she do?
Accept, but give the NPO a slightly lower rating
Accept, as long as she discloses it after the report is issued
Accept, because family relationships are irrelevant in social audit
Decline the engagement because of a conflict of interest that impairs independence
Independence is fundamental; a close relationship with management creates a conflict of interest that should lead to declining the engagement.
Social Impact Assessment & Assessors
What is the main purpose of social impact assessment for SSE-registered enterprises?
To provide investors and donors credible evidence of the social outcomes and impact achieved
To compute the enterprise's income-tax liability
To value the enterprise's shares for listing
To decide the coupon rate on ZCZP instruments
SIA verifies and reports the social impact achieved so that funders can rely on it.
Social Impact Assessment & Assessors
Which professional quality is most essential for a social impact assessor?
Ability to promote the enterprise to donors
Willingness to accept performance-linked fees from the enterprise
Objectivity and professional scepticism
Prior employment with the enterprise being audited
Assessors must be objective and sceptical; promotional roles or contingent fees would undermine independence.
Social Impact Assessment & Assessors
A social auditor collects beneficiary data and plans to publish names and phone numbers in the report as evidence. What is the appropriate approach?
Protect beneficiary privacy and use anonymised or aggregated data unless informed consent is obtained
Publish the details, since transparency overrides privacy
Sell the data to researchers to recover costs
Share the data with the NPO's marketing team
Confidentiality and data-protection principles require anonymisation and consent when handling beneficiary information.
Social Impact Assessment & Assessors
Which of the following is a key difference between social impact assessment and a statutory financial audit?
SIA is concerned only with the balance sheet
A financial audit measures outcomes for beneficiaries
SIA evaluates changes in the lives of beneficiaries, while a financial audit expresses an opinion on financial statements
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
SIA focuses on social outcomes and impact; a financial audit focuses on the truth and fairness of financial statements.
SIA Frameworks, Techniques & Standards
In the Social Return on Investment (SROI) method, an NPO invested ₹20 lakh and the present value of social benefits is estimated at ₹70 lakh. What is the SROI ratio?
SROI = present value of benefits ÷ value of inputs = 70 ÷ 20 = 3.5, i.e., ₹3.5 of social value per ₹1 invested.
SIA Frameworks, Techniques & Standards
In impact measurement, 'deadweight' refers to:
The cost of the programme's staff
The total number of beneficiaries
Outcomes displaced from one area to another
The outcome that would have happened even without the intervention
Deadweight estimates what would have occurred anyway and is deducted to avoid over-claiming impact.
SIA Frameworks, Techniques & Standards
Which of the following is a recognised catalogue of standardised impact metrics, maintained by the Global Impact Investing Network?
GAAP
Basel III
